passage: The client's email arrived on Tuesday evening: the totals in Sachin's analysis did not match their own records. My stomach dropped. I had handed over the whole quarterly report with a two-line brief and a single check-in, on the last day. For a week afterwards I doubted every delegation I had ever made, and my hand hovered over the next task, ready to just do it myself. Then I reread my own brief. It was vague, and the deadline left no room to look at a draft. So I sat down with Sachin, owned my part, and split the next job into three pieces with a Wednesday check-in for each. It came back clean. I still feel a small flinch when I hand something over, and I am learning to let it sit there. Kashish

qa.q: What did the client notice in the analysis Sachin prepared?
qa.a: The totals in Sachin's analysis did not match the client's own records.

qa.q: Why did Kashish's hand hover over the next task, ready to do it alone?
qa.a: Kashish doubted delegating after the failure and was tempted to take the work back, which the hesitation shows.

qa.q: What would you advise Kashish to do when handing over a large task again?
qa.a: Split it into smaller pieces with regular check-ins, as Kashish did, so that problems show up early.

qa.q: How might Sachin have experienced the vague two-line brief?
qa.a: Sachin may have been unsure what was expected and had little chance for feedback, so the mistake was not only Sachin's.

grounding: The narrator doubts delegating after a junior's failure, reviews the brief, and delegates again in smaller steps with check-ins.

passage: Thursday, 9:40 pm. Anand, you did it again. Rohit stopped by my desk at four and I spent forty minutes drawing little boxes on a notepad for him, laughing about the time I broke a whole workbook in my first year. Disha waited beside the printer with her question, and I said "later, okay?" Later never came. She left at six, clutching her laptop bag. Tonight I counted: Rohit got three long sessions this week, Disha got one two-minute reply. Her work is not worse, it is just slower to explain itself, and talking with her costs me more effort. Tomorrow: fifteen minutes each on the calendar, the same ask of both, a short written status. I will judge the drafts, not how easy the chat felt. A bit embarrassed writing this down.

qa.q: How many long sessions did Rohit get this week, according to Anand's count?
qa.a: Rohit got three long sessions this week.

qa.q: Why does Anand feel embarrassed while writing the entry?
qa.a: Anand has caught a bias: time went to the junior who felt comfortable, while Disha got one two-minute reply.

qa.q: What step does Anand plan for tomorrow?
qa.a: Put fifteen minutes each for Rohit and Disha on the calendar and ask both for the same short written status.

qa.q: How might Disha have felt leaving at six with her bag held to her chest?
qa.a: Disha may have felt overlooked and unsure whether her questions were welcome.

grounding: The narrator notices favouring the junior who feels like them, and plans equal time and the same expectations for both juniors.

passage: I'm Joseph, and I sit two desks from Anjali on the analytics team, so I saw a bit of this. After her review she went quiet for a few days, and I assumed she was just tired. Then on Friday I heard her knock on the manager's door and ask, quite politely, "Could you show me one example of a report that meets the bar? And what would you like me to hit by the end of next month?" The manager seemed surprised, then pulled up two old reports. Anjali took notes. Later, at the coffee machine, she said it had been hard not to just moan to us instead. I can't say what she felt; she smiled, but her shoulders stayed tight. Two weeks on, a short goals sheet is stuck above her monitor.

qa.q: What did Anjali ask the manager to show her?
qa.a: One example of a report that meets the bar.

qa.q: What might Anjali have been feeling, judging by her smile and tight shoulders?
qa.a: Possibly some tension or resentment behind a polite face, though Joseph admits the signs are hard to read.

qa.q: What could Anjali do if the goals sheet still leaves some points unclear?
qa.a: Ask the manager politely for another concrete example or a short check-in, as she did before.

qa.q: How might the manager have seen Anjali's request?
qa.a: The manager seemed surprised, which suggests they had not realised the bar was unclear and may see the request as a fair one.

grounding: A colleague observes a worker who feels unfairly judged asking respectfully for concrete examples and goals rather than complaining.

passage: "Rafiq, the invoices are missing again," I whispered at six, and then fixed it myself before our director's review, saying nothing. The first time, two months back, that felt like kindness. By the third time I noticed Rafiq had stopped double-checking anything, because I always would. That evening I saw that my cover was costing Rafiq the chance to learn, and it was making me a little dishonest with our director. So the next morning I asked Rafiq for ten minutes, laid out the three misses, and we built a checklist together. Then I told the director myself: there had been slips, Rafiq was owning them, and here was the fix. My heart was pounding. The director only asked to see the checklist. Jahnavi

qa.q: What was missing before the director's review?
qa.a: The invoices were missing.

qa.q: Why was Jahnavi's heart pounding when talking to the director?
qa.a: Jahnavi was nervous about admitting the earlier slips openly after keeping quiet, yet chose honesty anyway.

qa.q: What could Jahnavi do if Rafiq slips again?
qa.a: Point it out kindly, ask Rafiq to fix it and to tell the director, using the shared checklist.

qa.q: How might Rafiq have felt when Jahnavi laid out the three misses?
qa.a: Rafiq may have felt embarrassed to learn the covering had been noticed, but also glad to get a fair chance to learn.

grounding: The narrator has been covering a junior's mistakes, sees it blocks learning, and coaches the junior while staying honest with the director.

passage: Abebe stood in the operations manager's doorway holding a folder. Three deliveries to the same customer had gone out wrong, and the manager had just said it was Abebe's team, so Abebe's fault. Yara, the junior dispatcher, had made the errors and sat at her desk down the hall, pretending to read. "I own that I didn't catch the pattern sooner," Abebe said. "But I sat with Yara twice and went through the checklist, and here are the dates. She has been carrying sixty orders a day alone since March. I'd like a second person on the evening shift." The manager frowned at the folder, then said they would look at the rosters on Monday. Abebe never once blamed Yara aloud, and walked back down the hall with a tight jaw.

qa.q: How many times had Abebe sat with Yara to go through the checklist?
qa.a: Abebe sat with Yara twice.

qa.q: What does Abebe's tight jaw suggest as Abebe walks back down the hall?
qa.a: Abebe is tense and probably still stung by the blame, even after making a calm case.

qa.q: What did Abebe ask the manager for, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: A second person on the evening shift, because Yara had been carrying sixty orders a day alone.

qa.q: How might Yara have felt sitting at her desk pretending to read?
qa.a: Yara may have been anxious and ashamed, aware the errors were hers and unsure whether she would be blamed.

grounding: A boss blames a lead for a junior's failures, and the lead owns their part, shows the coaching given and asks for resourcing without blaming the junior.

passage: When Tanuja announced Karan's promotion in Monday's meeting, my face went hot and my pen stopped moving. I had led that client launch. I wanted to say something in front of everyone. Instead I said, "Congratulations, Karan," and walked to the stairwell to breathe. By evening the anger had dulled enough for me to open a notes file and list what I had actually done next to what the promotion criteria said. On Wednesday I asked Tanuja for fifteen minutes in a closed room and said, "Help me understand what was missing." The answer was partly fair and partly not. I am still deciding whether to stay. But I am glad it did not come out in the meeting. Nikita

qa.q: Where did Nikita go after congratulating Karan?
qa.a: Nikita walked to the stairwell to breathe.

qa.q: Why did Nikita's pen stop moving during the announcement?
qa.a: Nikita was hit by anger and shock at the news and wanted to speak out in front of everyone.

qa.q: What would you advise Nikita to do while deciding whether to stay?
qa.a: Weigh the facts in the notes file and Tanuja's explanation, and see whether there is a clear path to promotion.

qa.q: How might Tanuja have seen the private request for an explanation?
qa.a: Tanuja may have valued the calm, direct question, since it allowed an honest talk rather than a public confrontation.

grounding: The narrator burns with anger at a passed-over promotion, lets it settle, collects facts, asks privately for an explanation and weighs staying.

passage: I'm Zubin, and I sit across from Ritu on the finance team. Last month our director changed the bonus pool so that the newest hire got nothing, even though the hire had done most of the closing work. Everyone saw it. Ritu did not say a word in the meeting. But afterwards she stayed late, and I noticed her drafting an email, deleting it, and drafting it again. She asked me quietly whether others felt the same, and over chai we spoke to two colleagues. Three days later she sent the director a short, careful note listing the facts and asking how the split was decided. I can't tell you whether she was scared or just being thorough. She did say once, "Saying nothing has a cost too." We all need this job.

qa.q: What did Ritu send to the director three days later?
qa.a: A short, careful note listing the facts and asking how the split was decided.

qa.q: What might Ritu have been worried about while drafting and deleting the email?
qa.a: Possibly the risk to her job, since speaking up could cost her, though Zubin admits it is hard to tell whether she was scared or just thorough.

qa.q: What could Ritu do if the director does not reply?
qa.a: Ask calmly for a short meeting, keep her written record, and lean on the two colleagues who share the concern.

qa.q: How might the newest hire see the bonus change?
qa.a: The newest hire may feel the closing work went unrecognised and may hope someone speaks up.

grounding: An observer sees a colleague who knows a decision is unfair weigh the risk, find allies and raise it calmly in writing.

passage: Pranav here. I work in the same design team as Ishita, so I have watched this for months. Our manager always hands the new client pitches to Meera and asks her opinion first in reviews. Ishita's mockups get "fine, ship it." Last Thursday she stayed until eight and put a one-page summary of her project results on the shared drive, time saved and revisions cut, then mentioned it in the team update. After that she asked the manager what the criteria were for leading a pitch. The manager said "let's talk about it" and looked at the clock. Ishita went back to her desk, her mouth a thin line. I don't know if she felt small or just tired, but over lunch she told me she is giving it until the year-end review before she decides about moving on.

qa.q: What did Ishita put on the shared drive?
qa.a: A one-page summary of her project results, showing time saved and revisions cut.

qa.q: What does the thin line of Ishita's mouth suggest?
qa.a: She may feel let down or overlooked after the vague reply, though Pranav cannot be certain.

qa.q: What could Ishita do before the year-end review?
qa.a: Keep making her results visible and ask again, in writing, for clear criteria.

qa.q: How might the manager have seen the question about criteria?
qa.a: The manager may have been caught off guard, since they answered "let's talk about it" and glanced at the clock.

grounding: A colleague observes a worker who feels overlooked under a favouring manager making results visible, asking for criteria and considering moving on.

passage:
Tuesday, 9 pm
Gopika: how was the review
Sangeeta: he called me "the backbone of the team" 🙂
Sangeeta: then handed me the Kolkata vendor audit. on top of the two I already have
Gopika: that's the third extra thing this month no?
Sangeeta: yes. he said people who really care don't count hours
Sangeeta: I felt proud for a second and then I felt weird
Gopika: weird how
Sangeeta: like the praise is the salary 😅
Gopika: what does your offer letter say about scope
Sangeeta: checking
Sangeeta: the audit isn't in it
Sangeeta: I'll email him tonight. happy to take it if we agree what comes off my plate and by when
Gopika: good. keep it in writing

qa.q: What extra task did the manager hand Sangeeta after the review?
qa.a: The Kolkata vendor audit.

qa.q: Why did Sangeeta feel weird after feeling proud?
qa.a: Sangeeta began to suspect the praise was standing in for pay, since the manager linked caring about the team to not counting hours.

qa.q: What does Sangeeta plan to send the manager, and why is it useful?
qa.a: An email offering to take the audit if they agree what comes off the plate and by when, which sets the scope in writing.

qa.q: How might the manager see his own request?
qa.a: He may think he is offering trust and recognition, even though the effect is that Sangeeta carries unpaid hours.

grounding: A manager pairs praise with extra work and hints that loyalty means unpaid hours; the worker feels flattered and trapped, then sets limits in writing.

passage: Gurpreet, you asked why I still send my old manager a card every Diwali. Sit down; it is a longer story. I was twenty-four, and a client had just called my proposal careless. The whole room went quiet, and my manager said, "I have read every line of it, and I stand behind her." I nearly cried in the lift. I worked harder that year than ever. But listen: months later I spotted a wrong number in his own forecast, and I told him privately, even though it was awkward. He thanked me. That is what the gratitude taught me. I could owe him a great deal and still tell him the truth. Now go and read your own numbers once more. Madhuri

qa.q: How old was Madhuri when the client called her proposal careless?
qa.a: Madhuri was twenty-four.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri nearly cry in the lift?
qa.a: Madhuri was overwhelmed with relief and gratitude that her manager stood behind her when the room went quiet.

qa.q: What can Gurpreet learn about thanking a manager?
qa.a: Be grateful and work hard, yet still report an error privately, as Madhuri did with the wrong number in the forecast.

qa.q: How did Madhuri's manager likely see her private correction?
qa.a: He thanked her, which suggests he valued honest input more than silent loyalty.

grounding: An elder recalls a manager who backed her when others doubted her, and how her gratitude stayed alongside honesty about his error.
